components.gap: Durrett's own sigma-field definition and its stated reason are not supplied on the current route. Durrett (sec. 1.1, p. 1) defines a sigma-field as a nonempty collection closed under complements and countable unions, and says closure under countable intersections is left out of the definition so that it is easier to check. The entry (lines 26-37) instead requires the collection to contain Omega. It states neither the nonempty-collection form, nor its equivalence with the handbook form, nor that reason. Durrett's alternative name 'field' for an algebra (p. 4) is also absent from the entry and the route. Durrett's form and reason occur only in the uninput file handbook/parts/p15/limit-theorems-and-concentration-w02c-p15-014.tex.

components.gap: Durrett's Example 1.1.2 is titled 'Discrete probability spaces' (p. 2) and continues on p. 3 with the astragali. These are dice of ancient Egypt made from sheep ankle bones, coming to rest on four sides scored 1, 3, 4 and 6 with no reason to take the four outcomes as equally likely, so probabilities p1, p3, p4, p6 are needed. The theorem and its following text (lines 129-155; proof annex lines 92-145) supply the general construction and its converse, and the uniform finite case through the finite-probability chapter. They call the model a 'countable atomic model' and never give the source name 'discrete probability space'. The astragalus example is absent on the current route; it occurs only in the uninput file probability-spaces-and-random-variables-w02c-p15-002.tex.

components.gap: Durrett (pp. 16-17) defines almost sure convergence without a prescribed limit: Xn converges a.s. when P(Omega_o) = 1, where Omega_o is the set on which lim Xn exists. He sets X_infinity = limsup Xn so that a limit is defined on the whole space. He defines an extended random variable as a function on a set D in F with values in R* = [-inf, inf], measurable for script R*, the Borel sets of the usual topology generated by [-inf,a), (a,b) and (b,inf]. The entry (lines 302-321, with the line 237 convention that all functions are defined on all of Omega) defines a.s. convergence only to a specified real X and does not admit random variables defined on an event D. It equips the extended line with the sigma-algebra generated by [-inf,a] without identifying it with the order-topology Borel sets, and it omits the X_infinity = limsup convention. None of these source forms is supplied on the current route.

components.gap: Durrett concludes from Theorem 1.3.7 (p. 16) that Omega_o = {omega: lim Xn exists} = {limsup Xn - liminf Xn = 0} is a measurable set. The theorem and its following remark (lines 323-352; annex lines 276-339) supply measurability of inf, sup, liminf and limsup, and of {Xn -> X} for a given real X, and they note that limsup - liminf may be inf - inf. They never supply measurability of the existence set Omega_o itself in a well-defined form, and no on-route text does; it appears only in the uninput file probability-spaces-and-random-variables-w02c-p15-002.tex.

components.gap: The entry (lines 367-370) defines the point mass at x as the number P(X = x) and says that a point mass is a number. Durrett uses the term for a probability law. His Example 1.2.8, 'Point mass at 0' (p. 13), is the law with F(x) = 1 for x >= 0 and 0 for x < 0, the simplest discrete distribution. On p. 117 he calls the law at 1/n a point mass at 1/n. The source usage is neither recorded nor bridged, and Example 1.2.8 is not presented in the chapter, so a different meaning is substituted for a source term. The rest of the entry (law as pushforward, P(X in B), same law) matches p. 10.

components.gap: The pi-lambda part matches Durrett's Theorem A.1.4 (pp. 456-457). Durrett's uniqueness result, Theorem A.1.5 (pp. 457-458), concerns measures that agree on a pi-system P and admit An in P increasing to Omega with finite measure; its proof localizes to A in P. The entry (lines 410-415; annex lines 374-429) proves uniqueness only for two probability measures on (S, sigma(C)), which narrows the sigma-finite statement. The on-route measure-extension uniqueness covers only extensions of a sigma-finite premeasure on an algebra, not agreement on a pi-system, so Theorem A.1.5 is not supplied on the current route.
